description: LUNAV is a project that focuses on making lunar exploration more accessible by combining real astronomical data, 3D visualization, and mission analysis. Users can evaluate potential Moon landing sites, compare sunlight and Earth visibility, explore launch opportunities, and assess surface conditions and resources. We aim to turn complex space mission data into practical insights that support better planning and decision-making.
summary:
LUNAV is an interactive web application that helps mission planners, educators, and the public investigate landing conditions near the Moon’s south pole. We combine a 3D Earth–Moon viewer with terrain-aware analysis to make complex lunar data easier to interpret.

Users select a lunar destination, explore simulated flight opportunities, and assess estimated sunlight and direct-to-Earth visibility during a chosen surface stay. They can compare two locations at the same arrival time, examining illumination, communication windows, elevation, slope, and regional scientific context. Using NASA JPL’s SPICE toolkit and Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter elevation data, we calculate Sun and Earth directions and estimate when surrounding terrain obstructs them.

LUNAV addresses the challenge by bringing these calculations into a visual workflow. Understanding when a site may lose sunlight or its view of Earth helps users evaluate potential power and communication constraints. By visualizing these metrics and data LUNAV can provide an intuitive way to identify key landing sites.
details:
LUNAV is a web-based lunar landing-site navigator that helps users investigate where to land and what conditions to expect after arrival. We aim to visualize the surrounding terrain can obstruct sunlight and views of Earth influencing how a landing site is chosen. These conditions matter when considering solar power and direct communication with Earth.

Our goal is to help students, educators, and early-stage mission designers explore these trade-offs through an interactive Earth–Moon environment.

How it works

Users select an Earth launch site and a destination on the 3D Moon, then explore candidate flight opportunities and simulated transfer trajectories. After selecting a flight, they can examine estimated surface conditions using its arrival time as the starting point.

For a chosen surface stay, LUNAV estimates sunlight and Earth-visibility windows, displays elevation and local slope, and provides geological and regional hydrogen context. Users can select a second lunar location and compare both sites at the same arrival time and stay duration.

Behind these visualizations, we use NASA JPL’s SPICE toolkit to calculate the directions of the Sun and Earth relative to a lunar location. We combine those directions with lunar elevation data to estimate whether surrounding terrain blocks either object. This lets users investigate how local topography affects potential solar access and direct-to-Earth communication.

Benefits and intended impact

With LUNAV, users can:

  • Compare potential sites using consistent conditions.
  • Identify estimated periods of darkness or blocked Earth visibility.
  • Examine terrain and regional scientific context in one interface.
  • Explore lunar mission constraints without writing analysis code.

We aim to make NASA’s scientific data accessible while helping users understand why choosing a landing site requires balancing several competing needs.

Tools and technologies

  • SvelteKit & Svelte: Front-end development and user interface
  • CesiumJS: 3D lunar mapping and visualization
  • Python (FastAPI, NumPy, Rasterio, PyProj): Backend development, terrain processing, and scientific calculations
  • SpiceyPy & lamberthub: Orbital calculations and flight trajectory estimation
  • NASA JPL SPICE Kernels: Planetary positions and lunar orientation
  • NASA LRO (LOLA & LROC): Lunar elevation data and surface imagery
  • USGS Lunar Geologic Map: Lunar geological data and mapping
  • Lunar Hydrogen Dataset: Regional hydrogen distribution and resource analysis


AI and Generative Tools

We used AI tools throughout the project to accelerate development. Specifically:

  • Design: AI was used during brainstorming to explore different design concepts and evaluate possible approaches.
  • Debugging : AI assisted in identifying errors, understanding their causes, and finding appropriate solutions during development.

No NASA images, logo or branding was used as input or output in AI generation.
